concept.body: A solid of revolution is swept by spinning a flat region about an axis: a rectangle with one side on the axis sweeps a cylinder (width → radius, axis side → height); a right triangle with a leg on the axis sweeps a cone; a semicircle on its diameter sweeps a sphere. The axis choice changes the solid — identify radius (reach from axis) and height (run along axis) before any volume recall.

explanationVariants: The 4-side lies on the axis (height); the 2-width reaches out (radius).

widget.prompt: A 2-by-4 rectangle spins about its 4-unit side. Volume coefficient (of π) = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 32 spins about the 2-side (r = 4, h = 2, giving 32π) — the axis here is the 4-side: 16π.

steps.body: Slicing has a reverse gear: **revolution**. Spin a flat region about an axis and it sweeps a solid — the figure's rectangle (one side ON the axis) sweeps a cylinder whose radius is the rectangle's width and whose height is its length along the axis. Spin therefore MANUFACTURES the solids whose sections you just cataloged.

explanationVariants: Width 3 becomes the reach from the axis (radius); the 7-side lies along the axis (height).
Cylinder r = 3, h = 7: V = π(9)(7) = 63π (the formula from Grade 8).

widget.prompt: A 3-by-7 rectangle spins about its 7-unit side. The swept cylinder's volume = ? (exact multiple of π — enter the coefficient)

numericErrors.feedback: 21 = 3 × 7 forgets to square the radius — V = πr²h = π(9)(7) = 63π.
147 = π(49)(3)'s coefficient spins about the WRONG side — the 7-side is the axis, so r = 3: 63π.
126 doubles — the sweep counts the full circle once: π(9)(7) = 63π.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

explanationVariants: About the 12-leg: that leg is the height, the 5-leg reaches out as radius.

widget.prompt: A right triangle with legs 5 and 12 spins about its 12-unit leg. The swept cone's volume coefficient (of π) = ?

numericErrors.feedback: 240 spins about the 5-leg instead (r = 12, h = 5) — the stated axis is the 12-leg: ⅓(25)(12) = 100.
300 skips the ⅓ — a cone claims a third of its cylinder: 100.
60 = ⅓(5)(12)·? forgets to square r — ⅓(5²)(12) = 100.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: ⅓π(5²)(12) = 100π — and about the other leg it would be 240π: the axis is part of the problem.
widget.successFeedback: ⅓π(5²)(12) = 100π — and about the other leg it would be 240π: the axis is part of the problem.

explanationVariants: Rectangle → cylinder; right triangle (leg on axis) → cone; and the sphere needs a curved generator.
A SEMICIRCLE spun on its diameter sweeps the sphere.

widget.prompt: Which flat region, spun about the indicated axis, sweeps a SPHERE?

options.label: A semicircle, about its diameter
options.feedback: Half the disk sweeps the whole ball — each point traces its circle of latitude. (A FULL circle would sweep the same sphere twice over.)

options.label: A full circle, about a line outside it
options.feedback: An external axis sweeps a TORUS (a donut) — the sphere wants the semicircle on its own diameter.

options.label: A rectangle, about one side
options.feedback: That's the cylinder factory — spheres need the curved edge of the semicircle.

options.label: A right triangle, about a leg
options.feedback: That sweeps the cone — the sphere's generator is the semicircle.

widget.prompt: A semicircle of radius 6 spins about its diameter, sweeping a sphere. Set the radius and read the volume as a multiple of π.
widget.successFeedback: 288π. The sweep is what makes it a sphere: every point of the semicircle traces a circle, and (4/3)π(6³) = (4/3)(216)π = 288π. Revolution is not a new formula — it is where the formula comes from.
widget.lowFeedback: Smaller than the swept sphere. The semicircle has radius 6, so grow the radius toward it.
widget.highFeedback: Larger than the swept sphere. The semicircle has radius 6, so bring the radius back down.

commonBuilds.feedback: 36π is the sphere of radius 3 — half the radius gives an eighth of the volume, not half. Cubing is what makes the difference so large.
144π would be (2/3)π(6³), the hemisphere the semicircle sweeps only if it stopped halfway. A full spin about the diameter sweeps the whole sphere: 288π.

widget.prompt: A rectangle spins about an axis PARALLEL to one side but 2 units away (no contact). The swept solid is:

options.label: A hollow cylinder
options.feedback: The gap sweeps the hole: outer radius = far side's distance, inner = 2. Washers, stacked — a shape the composite-solids chapter will price by subtraction.

options.label: A solid cylinder
options.feedback: Solid needs the region to TOUCH the axis — the 2-unit gap hollows the core: a tube.

options.label: A cone
options.feedback: Cones need a slanted edge reaching the axis — a parallel offset rectangle sweeps the straight-walled tube.

options.label: A sphere
options.feedback: Spheres come from semicircles — this sweep is the ring-sectioned tube.

hints: The target cone has r = 9 and h = 12 — the spinning triangle's legs, with the h-leg on the axis.
The slant edge of the sweep is the triangle's hypotenuse.
explanationVariants: Legs 9 and 12 give hypotenuse √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15 — the cone's slant height.

widget.prompt: You need a cone of radius 9 and height 12 by revolution. The right triangle you spin has its 12-leg on the axis — how long is its hypotenuse (the cone's slant edge)?

numericErrors.feedback: 21 = 9 + 12 adds the legs — the hypotenuse is √(81 + 144) = 15.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: √(9² + 12²) = 15 — the generator's hypotenuse becomes the slant height.
widget.successFeedback: √(9² + 12²) = 15 — the generator's hypotenuse becomes the slant height.

takeaways: Rectangle (side on axis) → cylinder; right triangle (leg on axis) → cone; semicircle (diameter on axis) → sphere.
The AXIS is part of the problem: swapping legs swaps 100π for 240π.
Offset regions sweep holes — rings and tubes, priced later by subtraction.
